sources.title: Project-authored synthetic and generic-name cases
sources.description: Sentences written by the project to probe specific PERSON ambiguities. Names are compositions of generic given names and surnames, constructed names, or ordinary words; no sentence quotes, paraphrases or derives from any existing text.

license.terms_note: The repository has no license yet. Content is internal-only until the owner selects one; the public-release gate fails while this is true.

personal_data.notes: Generic or constructed names only. Resemblance to a real individual is coincidental and unavoidable for common names; no case is meant to depict a specific real person.

transformations: none: authored directly as canonical Case records
known_bias: Authored by a single author session: coverage reflects that author's judgment of what is confusable.
English cases favour US/UK naming conventions; Korean cases favour contemporary South Korean naming and do not cover North Korean or diaspora orthography.
Familiarity labels (common/rare/novel) are authored judgments, not measured against a name-frequency reference.

sources.title: US Census Bureau: Frequently Occurring Surnames from the 2010 Census
sources.description: Census Bureau tabulation of the 162,253 surnames occurring 100 or more times in the 2010 Census. Used only to derive a frequency band (common, rare or absent) for surname components cited by cases; no table rows, counts or ranks are stored in this repository.
sources.version: 2010 Census release, file Names_2010Census.csv inside names.zip (Last-Modified 2016-12-15); landing page last revised 2021-10-08

license.terms_note: Published by a US federal agency; US Government works are generally not subject to copyright in the United States. Not redistributed here regardless: the repository cites the table and stores only derived bands. Legal review of that reading is still pending.

personal_data.notes: Aggregate surname counts; the Census Bureau states the data do not identify individuals. Only band labels for surnames that cases cite are stored.

transformations: Reduced to one band label per cited surname component (common, rare or absent); counts, ranks and all other rows discarded
Surname normalized to ASCII letters a-z before lookup
known_bias: US-centric: surnames frequent in other English-speaking countries or in South Asian, African and East Asian communities can be rare here (for example Raman, Okafor).
Names are census returns as edited by the Bureau; transliteration variants are separate entries.
Surnames only: no given-name frequency is derived from this source.

sources.title: South Korean surname populations, 2015 census (Statistics Korea, KOSIS table DT_1IN15SD)
sources.description: 2015 population by surname from the Statistics Korea census table, read through the English Wikipedia list of Korean surnames at a pinned revision. Used only to derive a frequency band (common or rare) for Hangul surname components cited by cases; no population figures are stored in this repository.
sources.version: English Wikipedia revision 1377792072 of 'List of Korean surnames' (timestamp 2026-10-01); table note: total population 49,705,663, surnames of five or more people

license.terms_note: The Wikipedia text is CC BY-SA 4.0; the underlying figures are Statistics Korea census statistics. Neither is redistributed: the repository cites the revision and stores only derived band labels. Legal review of that reading is still pending.

personal_data.notes: Aggregate surname populations; no individual is identified. Only band labels for surnames that cases cite are stored.

transformations: Reduced to one band label per cited Hangul surname component (common or rare); populations and all other rows discarded
Table parsed from wikitext; 153 of the roughly 191 listed Hangul surnames were parsed, covering 49,609,870 of 49,705,663 people
known_bias: A secondary transcription of the KOSIS table, not the KOSIS file itself; transcription errors are possible.
Only part of the surnames in use were parsed, so absence from the parsed table proves nothing and no 'novel' Korean band is derived.
South Korea only: North Korean and diaspora surname distributions are not represented.

policy.attribution: English Wikipedia, 'List of Korean surnames' (pinned revision in the source version field), CC BY-SA 4.0; figures from Statistics Korea (KOSIS).

sources.title: Hangul Spelling Rules (한글 맞춤법), Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism Notice No. 2017-12
sources.description: Official Korean orthography. Cited for chapter 5 spacing: Article 41 (particles attach to the preceding word) and Article 48 (surname and given name are written together; titles and offices that follow are spaced; spacing a two-syllable surname is allowed where clarity needs it). Cases cite the article number; no rule text is copied.
sources.version: Hangul Spelling Rules in force from 2017-03-28 (Notice No. 2017-12), as served by the National Institute of Korean Language norms site

license.terms_note: A Korean government public notice; such notices appear not to be protected by copyright (Copyright Act of Korea, Article 7) but that reading has not been legally reviewed. Nothing is copied: cases cite article numbers only. The artifact digest is of the HTML page as served on the retrieval date and may change if the site changes.

personal_data.notes: Rule text about naming and spacing; contains no personal data. Examples in the rule that name historical persons are not reused: cases use synthetic names.

transformations: None applied to source text; only the article numbers are cited
Illustrative names in cases are authored, not taken from the rule's examples
known_bias: Describes standard written South Korean orthography; informal, chat and dialect spacing is not covered.
Spacing rules describe how names are written, not how they are tokenized or detected.

sources.title: Romanization of Korean (국어의 로마자 표기법), Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism Notice No. 2014-42
sources.description: Official Korean romanization rules. Cited for chapter 3: Article 3 (proper nouns start with a capital letter) and Article 4 (a personal name is written surname, space, given name; the given name is written together, with a hyphen between syllables permitted). Cases cite the article number; no rule text is copied.
sources.version: Romanization of Korean in force from 2014-12-05 (Notice No. 2014-42), as served by the National Institute of Korean Language norms site

license.terms_note: A Korean government public notice; such notices appear not to be protected by copyright (Copyright Act of Korea, Article 7) but that reading has not been legally reviewed. Nothing is copied: cases cite article numbers only. The artifact digest is of the HTML page as served on the retrieval date and may change if the site changes.

personal_data.notes: Rule text about naming and spacing; contains no personal data. Examples in the rule that name historical persons are not reused: cases use synthetic names.

transformations: None applied to source text; only the article numbers are cited
Illustrative names in cases are authored, not taken from the rule's examples
known_bias: The rule recommends a form; real romanized names also use older systems, passport spellings and personal preferences (Article 7 allows established spellings).
It says how to write a name, not how a text will spell it.

sources.title: Personal names around the world, W3C Internationalization (i18n) article
sources.description: W3C i18n article describing how personal names differ: patronymics, family-name-first order, multiple family names with linking words, middle initials, honorific and title stacking. Cited for the structure of multi-part names; cases cite the section; no article text is copied and the article's example names are not reused.
sources.version: First published 2011-08-17; page served with Last-Modified 2024-12-17

license.terms_note: W3C documents are published under the W3C Document License. Nothing is copied: cases cite section headings only. Legal review of that use is pending.

personal_data.notes: Descriptive article; it names a few real people as examples. None of those names is reused in cases, which use synthetic names built on the same patterns.

transformations: None applied to source text; only section headings are cited
Illustrative names in cases are authored; the article's example names are not reused
known_bias: An English-language overview with a small set of cultures; it does not cover every naming system.
Describes how names are structured, not how a text will punctuate or order them.
